standard_prerequisites.name: Propositional truncation
standard_prerequisites.statement: The truncation of a type is a mere proposition, and to prove a mere proposition from a truncation it suffices to assume an untruncated witness.
standard_prerequisites.use: It is what makes the truncation in the statement and the two truncation inductions of the proof (source lines 787 and 794) legitimate.

standard_prerequisites.name: Characterisation of paths in Sigma types
standard_prerequisites.statement: A path between pairs is a pair of a path between the first components and a path between the transported second components.
standard_prerequisites.use: It is used at source line 784 to compute the identity type of the type X.

standard_prerequisites.name: Univalence and idtoeqv
standard_prerequisites.statement: Identity of types is equivalent to equivalence of types, so a path between types may be described by an equivalence.
standard_prerequisites.use: It is used at source line 784 to turn the identity type (A,p) = (B,q) into the type of equivalences A equiv B.

standard_prerequisites.name: Mere proposition, set and 1-type
standard_prerequisites.statement: A mere proposition has all its identity types contractible, a set has all its identity types mere propositions, and a 1-type has all its identity types sets.
standard_prerequisites.use: These three levels are exactly what the proof compares at source lines 785, 787-788 and 795.

core_obligations: Define X as the type of pairs (A,p) with A a type and p a truncation witness that A is merely equal to the two-element type, and let x0 be the pair of the two-element type with the truncation of reflexivity (source line 783).

Show the identity type x0 = x0 of X is equivalent to the equivalences of the two-element type with itself, using the characterisation of paths in Sigma types, the fact that the truncation witness is a mere proposition, and univalence; conclude that X is not a set (source lines 784-785).

Show that every type A occurring in a pair of X is a set, by truncation induction on the witness that A is merely equal to the two-element type together with the fact that the two-element type is a set; since equivalences between sets are sets, every identity type of X is a set, so X is a 1-type (source lines 787-788).

Define the family Y(x) as the identity type x0 = x; by the previous step each Y(x) is a set, and the truncation witness carried by x gives an element of the truncation of Y(x), so the product over x of the truncation of Y(x) holds (source lines 789-792).

From the truncated conclusion derive a contradiction: the empty type is a mere proposition, so one may assume an actual section of Y, which makes X a mere proposition and therefore a set, contradicting the second step (source lines 793-795).

proof_roadmap.step: Build the type X of types merely equal to the two-element type and its base point.
Identify the loop space of X with the equivalences of the two-element type and conclude X is not a set.
Show X is a 1-type and choose the path family Y(x) := (x0 = x).
Inhabit the truncated hypothesis and derive the contradiction from the truncated conclusion.

difficulty_reason: Counted unit is the labelled lemma thm:no-higher-ac at source lines 779-781: there is a type X and a family Y over it, each Y(x) a set, for which the truncated choice principle (3.8.3) fails. The author's proof (source lines 782-796) manufactures the counterexample instead of quoting one, and the two facts required of X pull in opposite directions: univalence together with the characterisation of paths in Sigma types makes the loop space at the base point equivalent to the equivalences of the two-element type with itself, which is what shows X is not a set (source lines 784-785), while truncation induction on the witness that A is merely equal to the two-element type shows that every A occurring in X is a set and hence that X is a 1-type (source lines 787-788). The statement shows neither that the family has to be the path type to the base point nor that the contradiction is reached by observing that an actual section would make X a mere proposition (source lines 793-795).
